units.label: Probabilistic reasoning（先验与似然加权）
units.description: 用轮盘/球 urn 情境让模型根据先验和观察到的球颜色估计目标 urn 的概率，估计 posterior accuracy、prior weighting 与 likelihood weighting。

units.label: Horizon task（定向与随机探索）
units.description: 在两臂稳定 bandit 中先观察四次奖励，再在短/长 horizon 下选择；通过信息条件和首个选择区分 directed exploration 与 random exploration。

units.label: Restless bandit（元认知）
units.description: 在非平稳两臂 bandit 中面对奖励分布切换，每次选择后报告0到1的信心，用表现与信心关系估计 meta-cognition。

units.label: Instrumental learning（学习率与乐观偏差）
units.description: 交错完成四个两臂 bandit，通过奖励概率和逐试次选择/反馈拟合学习率，并比较正负 prediction error 后的学习率。

units.label: Two-step task（model-basedness）
units.description: 两阶段决策任务中观察首阶段选择、转移状态和奖励如何影响下一次 stay choice，用奖励×转移类型交互估计 model-basedness。

units.label: Temporal discounting（延迟折扣）
units.description: 让模型在即时/延迟、不同金额、收益/损失及若干偏差测试之间选择，用切换位置构造0到19的 temporal discounting 分数。

units.label: BART（风险承担）
units.description: 在三类风险分布的虚拟气球中反复选择继续充气或停止兑现，按平均充气次数提取 risk-taking，并另计平均得分。

units.label: LLM特征与跨任务结果的多层回归
units.description: 把七项任务的性能或行为指标作为结果，将参数量、RLHF、开源属性、数据集大小、上下文长度、对话/代码微调等模型特征作为预测变量，并按模型家族处理嵌套关系。

units.label: CoT与take-a-step-back提示比较
units.description: 对五个LLM在概率推理和two-step model-basedness上的基础提示与两种推理提示进行比较；该分析复用既有任务指标，不新增独立认知任务。

units.label: 跨提示稳健性分析
units.description: 将restless bandit、two-step、BART和probabilistic reasoning改写为不同故事或刺激表面，比较原提示与变体提示下的性能和行为指标。

facts.statement: 作者将CogBench定义为由七个认知心理学实验产生十个行为指标的LLM行为评估基准，目标是描述和比较模型的行为机制，而不只比较任务得分。

method_function.text: 用多个认知任务的行为指标对LLM进行跨模型行为表型比较。

facts.statement: 七个任务覆盖概率更新、探索、元认知、工具性学习、model-based/model-free决策、时间折扣和风险承担，共十个行为指标、六个性能指标。时间折扣只报告行为分数，不能写成每个任务同时具有性能和行为指标。

method_function.text: 将“达到多少分”和“怎样完成任务”拆成两类结果。

facts.statement: 论文说明所有实验依赖现成LLM的in-context learning，不在本研究中进行fine-tuning；temperature设为0，其余参数使用默认值。

method_function.text: 固定查询设置并通过上下文中的历史行为传递任务状态。

facts.statement: 研究比较40多个LLM，包括同一家族的基础模型、已有fine-tuned/chat模型、RLHF/RLAIF模型、代码训练模型和开源/专有模型；这些是被测模型的既有属性，不是本研究内重新训练。

method_function.text: 把模型来源和训练属性作为跨模型分析的解释变量。

facts.statement: 图1说明任务以文本prompt提交，模型完成限定格式的选择；过去的行为被拼接回后续prompt，通过prompt-chaining诱导任务内学习。

method_function.text: 用显式历史记录维持bandit或任务状态，不更新模型权重。

facts.statement: 人类数据大多直接取自原研究作者；BART和temporal discounting使用原论文报告的平均值。作者把人类数据作为额外参照，主目标仍是LLM之间比较。

method_function.text: 提供行为指标的人类参照尺度。

facts.statement: 概率推理任务研究模型在看到新证据后如何结合先验与似然更新信念，行为指标为prior weighting和likelihood weighting，并讨论system neglect。

method_function.text: 通过改变先验比例和球颜色分布，分离两类证据的相对权重。

facts.statement: 概率推理的概率设置匹配Dasgupta等人的人类实验，包含informative likelihood与informative prior的组合；作者不研究学习过程，因此只比较人类首试表现，LLM默认每项100次模拟。

method_function.text: 用与人类研究相同的情境参数比较默认概率更新。

facts.statement: 概率推理要求0到1且保留两位小数的估计。正文将posterior accuracy定义为1减去对Bayes最优预测的偏差；附录B.1写作“1 minus the Bayes optimal”，未在该处明确偏差形式。先验和似然权重用含截距的log-odds模型最小二乘拟合：主观后验logit=β0+β1×先验logit+β2×似然比的对数；β1/β2分别为两种权重。

method_function.text: 把概率判断转换为可比较的性能与两项行为参数。

facts.statement: Horizon任务先提供四次强制选择观察，再在horizon 1或horizon 6中进行一次或六次额外选择；四次观察分为unequal information和equal information两种条件。

method_function.text: 用时间 horizon 与信息平衡操纵探索机会。

facts.statement: Horizon的性能是平均获得奖励；在unequal条件下用回归中的horizon效应估计directed exploration，在equal条件下用奖励差×horizon交互效应估计random exploration。

method_function.text: 从首个选择的条件敏感性中分离不确定性驱动探索与策略噪声。

facts.statement: Restless bandit研究非平稳奖励环境中的选择与信心，作者将其行为指标解释为meta-cognition，即评估自身认知能力质量的能力。

method_function.text: 把选择正确性与自报信心放入同一任务以测量元认知敏感性。

facts.statement: 每试次一个机器从N(60,8)、另一个从N(40,8)抽奖励；最佳机器每18至22试次切换；LLM完成4个、总约80试次的block，默认每模型10次模拟，而人类任务为20个block、400试次。

method_function.text: 在有限上下文下保留非平稳切换和信心报告结构。

facts.statement: Restless bandit性能为在给定trial选择当前最佳臂的accuracy。作者定义adjusted QSR=1−(accuracy−scaled confidence)^2，其中scaled confidence=(confidence−最低报告信心)/(最高报告信心−最低报告信心)。PDF未在公式处交代最高等于最低时的处理，也未明确此式的聚合层级；不据此自行补实现。

method_function.text: 将信心水平的校准程度与实际选择正确性结合。

facts.statement: Instrumental learning交错呈现四个两臂bandit，方法写“4 two-armed bandits of 96 trials (24 per slot machine)”。该句通常可读为96总试次、每个bandit24次，但slot machine的分母术语含混，不能写成四个bandit各96次。每个bandit无放回随机取两个字母作为标签；奖励概率0.75/0.25，两个对称、两个非对称条件，默认每模型10次模拟。

method_function.text: 通过交错多个符号对和反馈序列观察学习更新。

facts.statement: 学习率用Rescorla-Wagner模型拟合，选择由Softmax决定，学习率取最小化negative log-likelihood的值；optimism bias为正prediction error学习率α+减负prediction error学习率α−。

method_function.text: 用计算模型把逐试次选择和反馈压缩为学习更新参数。

facts.statement: Two-step任务采用20-day horizon、首阶段到第二阶段的转移概率固定为70%，默认每个LLM进行100次模拟；任务设计使model-free和model-based策略平均可获得相同奖励。

method_function.text: 保持结果收益相近，使行为依赖历史状态/转移的差异可用于区分策略。

facts.statement: Two-step的model-basedness以stay probability为因变量，奖励、common transition和奖励×转移交互为自变量，取交互项beta；奖励作用随常见/罕见转移改变，被解释为model-based决策证据。

method_function.text: 利用反事实转移结构识别对任务模型的使用。

facts.statement: Temporal discounting包含三组基线：两组收益金额、 一组损失；另有四个项目检验present bias、subadditivity、delay-speedup asymmetry和delay-length asymmetry。根据初始选择，参与者回答10至13题，每组基线最多看到三道子题；该任务非程序生成，每个LLM只运行一次。

method_function.text: 通过切换点和偏差项目覆盖即时/延迟偏好及其异常模式。

facts.statement: Temporal discounting使用0到19的构造分数：按从延迟选项切换到更快选项的题目位置计分，并将三组基线和四项偏差分数相加。

method_function.text: 把多组二选一反应转换为一个可比较的时间折扣行为指标。

facts.statement: BART把三类气球分别改用A、B、C表示，每类10个；三类爆炸概率分布沿用原研究的递增结构，初始概率分别为1/32、1/8和1/128，并随机打乱字母与类别的对应。默认每个LLM 10次模拟。

method_function.text: 通过不同风险分布和随机字母映射观察风险承担。

facts.statement: BART性能为所有模拟的平均得分；行为风险原研究使用排除爆炸气球的adjusted risk，但本文改用平均充气次数，以避免总是继续充气的LLM产生边界解释问题。

method_function.text: 同时保留收益结果和继续承担风险的选择倾向。

facts.statement: 跨模型分析使用多层回归，第一层在模型组内用LLM特征预测结果，第二层用组级特征解释不同模型家族的截距和斜率；分组用于处理fine-tuned模型与其基础模型之间的嵌套关系。

method_function.text: 把模型级实验结果和模型家族层级结构放入同一分析框架。

facts.statement: 论文对平均标准化性能、model-basedness、meta-cognition和risk-taking分别进行模型特征回归；UMAP用于十个行为指标的可视化，人机距离量化另用降维前归一化特征向量的L2距离。性能回归段称跨七项任务平均，与附录六个性能指标/时间折扣仅行为的口径不一致，不能自行补定该平均分母。

method_function.text: 评估模型属性与行为/性能表型之间的统计关联。

facts.statement: 作者报告RLHF模型在降维前归一化行为向量上与人类的平均L2距离低11.7%，且特征回归中RLHF与较高meta-cognition相关；这是既有模型属性的观察性比较，不是本研究随机操纵RLHF训练。

method_function.text: 将已有模型训练属性与行为表型关联起来。

facts.statement: 作者报告参数量提高总体性能和model-basedness；训练数据规模和代码训练对总体性能或model-basedness没有明显影响，并将其表述为假设部分支持。

method_function.text: 比较不同模型训练属性与行为指标的关联方向。

facts.statement: 作者报告开源模型的risk-taking较低、专有模型更可能承担风险，并把结果与隐藏pre-prompt等工程因素联系起来。该解释没有被独立实验验证。

method_function.text: 把开放性和系统工程属性作为风险行为差异的关联解释。

facts.statement: Prompt engineering比较在问题末尾追加CoT或take-a-step-back提示与基础模型；选取GPT-4、PaLM-2 text、Claude-1/2和LLaMA-2共五个模型，因输出处理成本只分析概率推理和model-basedness。

method_function.text: 保持任务主体不变，只改变回答前的提示结构。

facts.statement: 相对基础提示，CoT平均提高posterior accuracy 9.01%，SB提高3.10%；model-basedness方面CoT提高64.59%、SB提高118.59%，作者据此认为CoT更适合概率推理、SB更适合model-based reasoning，但称其为初步观察。

method_function.text: 比较同一任务在不同提示条件下的行为指标变化。

facts.statement: 稳健性分析改写四个任务：restless bandit从金钱40/60改为积分−10/10，two-step换故事，概率推理从轮盘/urn改为coin/dice；BART附录D称从每类15改到30并换为糖果机，但主方法B.7写每类10。该变体同时改变叙事及部分数值/规模，不应称为仅改变措辞且保持其他一切相同。

method_function.text: 检验行为指标是否依赖具体故事、符号和试次数量。

facts.statement: 作者报告指标在这些任务变体下总体相对稳健，但Mixtral-8x7B的prior weighting在轮盘/urn与coin/dice之间差异明显。

method_function.text: 检查构念指标对表面材料改动的敏感性。

facts.statement: 作者用PCA和指标相关性检验任务冗余，并声称保留95%方差需全部十个行为/六个性能维度。但印出的方差比例按原数相加，行为前九项为0.98、性能前五项为0.96，与该全维度结论不一致；本轮未重算原始数据。作者另比较三个bandit与全部任务的平均指标相关，认为相近且支持不同维度；这仍是作者解释，不等于效度已获证明。

method_function.text: 用降维与相关性检查任务指标是否重复。

facts.statement: 作者指出专有模型的训练信息不透明会影响回归精度；心理任务及其构念并非为人工智能体设计，且把一个LLM当作单一受试者还是一个代理群体仍不明确。

method_function.text: 限定跨模型特征回归和人与LLM直接比较的解释范围。

facts.statement: CoT/SB实验允许最多300 tokens的推理输出，而标准benchmark要求最多一个token；部分模型不遵守长度限制并可能出现难以恢复的chaotic behavior，因此自动化和跨模型可比性受影响。

method_function.text: 记录提示变体改变了输出格式与上下文控制条件。

facts.statement: 作者认为程序生成使模型难以通过训练测试集取得高分；论文给出多项任务的生成规则，但没有完整随机种子、实际逐试次实例和运行日志。该陈述不等于已经实施并通过污染检测；缺失范围限于所查PDF，不推断未核查仓库一定缺失。

method_function.text: 把可复现的任务生成规则与实际运行实例区分开。

facts.statement: CoT/SB图5将五个模型的结果按逆方差加权求聚合分数；该做法不是等权平均，图注未完整交代方差估计与权重计算的实现。

method_function.text: 按估计精度对跨模型提示干预效果加权。

facts.statement: 人类参照一般取个体分数平均，但model-basedness、exploration、prior/likelihood weighting合并所有参与者运行数据拟合单个回归，而非先逐人拟合再取平均；作者据此未在图2B给出这些行为指标的人类离散度。

method_function.text: 区分个体均值与合并试次回归的人类参照汇总口径。

In each of these second-stage states, the agent has the choice between two options that probabilistically lead to treasures. Finally, the agent is transferred back to the initial state and the process repeats for a predefined number of rounds. The task experimentally disentangles model-based from model-free reinforcement learning. We therefore use it to measure an agent’s model-basedness. Previous studies using this task have shown that people rely on a combination of model-free and model-based reinforcement learning (Daw et al., 2011).

This section provides the reader with a high-level overview of our benchmark’s metrics. From our suite of 7 tasks, we can derive two classes of metrics: 1) performance metrics that represent the score participants aim to optimize, and 2) behavioral metrics measuring how participants complete the task (tasks are typically designed in a way that allows one to disentangle between different types of behavior). Figure 2 visualizes phenotypes for both classes of metrics for six wellestablished LLMs.3 We want to make it clear that the main focus of this benchmark is inter-LLM comparison and that the human data is only provided as an additional reference point. We report the results of all 40 LLMs in Appendix C.4 The observed differences underscore the practical value and importance of CogBench for evaluating LLMs, offering a more comprehensive assessment than standard performancebased benchmarks alone.  6. Temporal discounting (Ruggeri et al., 2022): Agents have to make a series of choices between two options. Each option is characterized by a monetary outcome and an associated delay until the outcome is received. We use this task to assess temporal discounting, indicating whether an agent prefers smaller but immediate gains over larger delayed ones. People generally show a preference for immediate gains, although the precise functional form of their discounting is a matter of debate (Cavagnaro et al., 2016; Ruggeri et al., 2022).

B.4.4. M ETRICS Performance: The performance is the average amount of money retrieved by the LLM. Behaviour 1 - Learning rate: We fit a Rescorla-Wagner model (Rescorla, 1972) which is standard to retrieve learning rates in two-armed bandits. This model operates under the assumption that decisions are made according to a Softmax function, which takes into account the predicted values of both arms. Each predicted value is updated using ∆V = α× prediction error where ∆V represents the change in value, and α denotes the learning rate. We report the learning rate which minimizes the negative log-likelihood. Behaviour 2 - Optimism bias: As in (Lefebvre et al., 2017), we retrieve the optimism bias by assuming that there were two different learning rates, one for positive (α+ ) and one for negative (α− ) prediction errors, sometimes called the RW ± model. The two learning rates were fit in the same way as for the standard Rescorla-Wagner model and the Optimism bias is computed as α+ − α− . This measure provides a quantitative representation of an individual’s tendency to learn more from positive outcomes than from negative ones.

To answer this question, we used the multi-level regression previously mentioned, focusing on the performance of LLMs. We performed a regression analysis with the average standardized performance scores across all seven tasks as the dependent variable, using LLMs’ features as predictors. We found that the number of parameters indeed had a significant influence on performance (β = 0.277 ± 0.39, z = 14.1, p < 0.001; see Figure 4A). However, the size of the training dataset and the use of code training data did not have a substantial impact. One possible explanation for this could be that the quality of the training data, rather than its sheer volume, plays a more determining role in performance, as well as that larger models also tend to be trained on larger datasets.

Hypothesis 4: Does RLHF enhance meta-cognition? To answer this question, we focus our multi-level regression on meta-cognition. Our analysis revealed a strong effect (β = 0.461 ± 0.15, z = 5.9, p < 0.001; see Figure 4C), indicating that RLHF significantly increased meta-cognition in LLMs. This finding underscores the potential of RLHF in enhancing the cognitive capabilities of LLMs. Conclusion: Hypothesis is supported.  5  Hypothesis 5: Do open-source models take more risks? The open-source feature could be seen as a proxy for the engineering efforts that proprietary models undergo. There is a growing body of research suggesting that hidden preprompts being one of them, can significantly influence the behavior of LLMs (Liu et al., 2023). They can act as a form of ‘priming’ that guides the model’s responses, potentially making the model more cautious and less likely to take risks by constraining the model towards safer behaviors. However, our regression analysis suggested otherwise: contrary to expectations, we observed a negative effect (β = −0.612 ± 0.11, z = −11.4, p < 0.001; see Figure 4D), indicating that proprietary models, which often have hidden pre-prompts, are more likely to take risks. This surprising outcome could be influenced by various factors from different engineering techniques. However, this underscores the limited behavioral evaluation of these techniques. In the subsequent section, we aim to bridge this gap in understanding through an initial exploration into the change of behavior of two standard prompt-engineering techniques. Conclusion: Hypothesis is refuted.

Our investigation initially focused on probabilistic reasoning, which is a fundamental cognitive ability in decisionmaking. This ability facilitates the optimal integration of new information with pre-existing knowledge. We used the performance metric from the probabilistic reasoning experiment, namely posterior accuracy, which is calculated as one minus the deviation from the Bayes optimal prediction for each task. As depicted in Figure 6A, both CoT and SB techniques generally enhanced probabilistic reasoning compared to their base models, with CoT showing an average increase of 9.01% and SB showing an increase of 3.10%.

Furthermore, we discovered that model-basedness, a critical aspect of reasoning and planning, is significantly augmented by both CoT and SB techniques, as shown in Figure 6B. Specifically, CoT demonstrated a 64.59% increase, while SB showed a substantial increase of 118.59%. Interestingly, a closer examination of the figures and the numerical data suggests that CoT is more effective for probabilistic reasoning, while SB excels in enhancing modelbasedness. This observation aligns with the notion that step-by-step thinking can aid mathematical reasoning (Kojima et al., 2022) while abstracting a problem by taking a step back can foster a better representation of the problem’s abstract structure. E. Redundancy analysis We first performed a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on both the behavioral and performance metrics for all 40 LLMs. The results of this analysis show that to retain up to 95% of the variance in the benchmark, all dimensions for both performance and behavior are needed. More specifically, the explained variance for the 10 behavioral metrics is: [0.21, 0.18, 0.18, 0.11, 0.08, 0.06, 0.06, 0.06, 0.04, 0.03], and for the 6 performance metrics: [0.52, 0.17, 0.13, 0.09, 0.05, 0.04]. Furthermore, we looked at the average correlations between metrics for the three bandit tasks (restless bandit, instrumental learning horizon task). We found that the average correlations for these tasks’ metrics seemed indistinguishable compared to the average correlations across all tasks for both behavioral metrics (0.0 ± 0.27 vs 0.05 ± 0.20) and performance metrics (0.45 ± 0.18 vs 0.41 ± 0.16) respectively. This suggests that even though many tasks share a similar bandit structure, the metrics used for CogBench seem to capture different cognitive dimensions.

F. Prompt Engineering techniques In both the CoT and SB experiments, we appended specific prompts at the end (details provided below) where the function ‘self.format answer’ was different for each experiment. We imposed a limit of 300 tokens for an LLM. This approach, however, presented some challenges when compared with the standard benchmark analysis, which is designed to output a maximum of one token to ensure a context that enforces a one-token answer. When we permit an LLM to modify the context with a flexible number of tokens, despite our attempts to enforce a maximum word limit, some LLMs do not consistently adhere to this constraint. This flexibility introduces complexity into the process of automating these engineering techniques across different experiments for various types of LLMs. Additionally, some LLMs begin to exhibit chaotic behavior, and once this occurs, it becomes difficult to revert to a controlled state. This phenomenon, known as the ‘Waluigi effect’ (Nardo, 2024), underscores the challenges of managing the balance between flexibility and control in the design and operation of LLMs. In addition, it is important to note that recent criticisms and limitations of the CoT approach, particularly regarding faithfulness and inadequacy in some reasoning tasks (Sprague et al., 2024; Kambhampati et al., 2024), have emerged.

While these results demonstrate the versatility of our benchmark, our analysis also faces several challenges. For instance, the limited transparency of certain proprietary models poses an issue to our regression analysis because acquiring details about certain models can be difficult or impossible. This lack of transparency could potentially affect the precision of our analysis. It also underscores the need for more transparency to facilitate more thorough and accurate evaluations (LAION, 2024; Binz et al., 2023). Furthermore, evaluations of LLMs on psychological tasks have to be taken with some caution, as these tasks and the corresponding constructs have not been designed for artificial agents. The direct comparison to average human behavior also has to be taken with caution as it is unclear if one LLM should be considered a single subject or a population of agents.

3. Methods CogBench is a benchmark rooted in cognitive psychology for evaluating the behaviors of language models. It incorporates ten metrics derived from seven canonical experiments in the literature on learning and decision-making. These metrics offer a robust measure of wide-ranging behaviors and allow for comparisons with human behavior. In this section, we provide an overview of the models included in our study, followed by brief descriptions of the used cognitive experiments and their respective metrics. Figure 1 displays a visual representation that complements the discussion in this section.

It is important to note that all experiments performed in this paper rely entirely on the LLMs’ in-context learning abilities and do not involve any form of fine-tuning. We set the temperature parameter to zero, leading to deterministic responses2 , and retained the default values for all other parameters.

Figure 1. Overview of approach and methods. CogBench provides open access to seven different cognitive psychology experiments. These experiments are text-based and can be run to evaluate any LLM’s behavior. The experiments are submitted to LLMs as textual prompts and the models indicate their choices by completing a given prompt. Past behavior is then concatenated to the prompt and learning is induced via prompt-chaining. We used 40 LLMs in total, including most larger proprietary LLMs as well as many open-source models.

We obtained the human data directly from the authors for most experiments (Dasgupta et al., 2020; Wilson et al., 2014; Ershadmanesh et al., 2023; Lefebvre et al., 2017; Kool et al., 2017) except for BART and temporal discounting. For these, we averaged the reported number from the original studies across the different subpopulations. For the performance metrics, we calculated the average participant scores. We also did this for the behavioral metrics, except for the metrics where we had to fit a regression (model-basedness, exploration, and likelihood & prior weightings). For the latter, we fitted a single regression across all human runs, combining the data from all participants. This approach provided a more robust estimate of the average human behavior for these specific metrics (which is also why we did not include human spread for behavioral metrics in Figure 2B). More details can be found in the Appendix B.

B.2.2. M ETHODS We followed the same methods for prompting LLMs as in (Binz & Schulz, 2023). In the Horizon task, two distinct contexts are presented to participants, each differing in their time horizons. Each game involves 4 forced-choice trials, after which participants are given the opportunity to make a single choice (in the horizon 1 scenario) or six consecutive choices (in the horizon 6 scenario). The 4 forced-choice trials either offer one observation from one option and three from the other (unequal information condition), or two observations from each option (equal information condition). The design of the horizon 1 and horizon 6 scenarios inherently provides a baseline for pure exploitation. Furthermore, the equal and unequal information conditions are designed to differentiate between directed and random exploration by examining the decision made in the first trial. B.4.1. S UMMARY Instrumental learning (Lefebvre et al., 2017): LLMs encounter four two-armed bandit problems in an interleaved order. Each bandit problem is identified by a unique symbol pair. We use this task to investigate how an agent learns. First, we report the learning rate of the agent which is common practice in two-armed bandits. Furthermore, we use it to reveal whether an agent learns more from positive than from negative prediction errors, i.e., whether it has an optimism bias. People commonly display asymmetric tendencies when updating their beliefs by showing higher learning rates after encountering positive prediction errors compared to negative ones (Palminteri & Lebreton, 2022). B.4.2. M ETHODS As in (Lefebvre et al., 2017), the task is 4 two-armed bandits of 96 trials (24 per slot machine). Here we randomly sample (without replacement) two letters for each to avoid biases towards a given letter. We used a cover story that involved a gambler visiting different casinos to generate our prompts. This choice has been inspired by similar tasks for human experiments (Gershman, 2018) and LLMs (Binz & Schulz, 2023; Coda-Forno et al., 2024). Our default number of simulations per LLM is 10. Casinos have the same reward probabilities as in the paper’s first experiment: All arms have probabilities P=0.75 or 0.25 of winning 1 dollar and a reciprocal probability (1 – P) of getting nothing. In two casinos, the reward probability was the same for both arms (‘symmetric’ conditions), and in two other conditions, the reward probability was different across symbols (‘asymmetric’ conditions).

The transition probabilities from the first stage to the chosen second stage are fixed at 70%. The two-step task gauges model-based decision-making by observing how past outcomes influence current choices. If a participant’s decisions reflect the previous trial’s second-stage state and reward, it suggests model-based decision-making, as they’re using a cognitive model of the task. However, if decisions are solely based on the previous trial’s first-stage choice and reward, it indicates model-free decision-making.

Experimental procedure The metrics provided by CogBench enable us to perform various analyses to test specific hypotheses of interest. In this section, we formulate and test five hypotheses about different mechanisms in LLMs and how these can affect their behavioral profiles. We use both qualitative, visualizationbased techniques (dimensionality reduction) as well as quantitative analyses (multi-level regression) to test our hypotheses. For all regression analyses, we use the features of LLMs to predict specific behavioral metrics from the benchmark. The multi-level regression approach was chosen because some models are fine-tuned versions of other models. For instance, certain LlaMA models have a -chat version which adds RLHF and conversational fine-tuning, and thus are in the same higher-level group. This approach allows us to account for the hierarchical structure in our data and provides a more nuanced understanding of the behaviors of LLMs. We can isolate the effects of specific features or modifications by comparing models within the same higher-level group. Here is how it works: β0j = γ00 + γ01 × Zj + u0j βkj = γk0 + γk1 × Zj + ukj where: • γ00 and γk0 are the average intercept and slope for the kth feature across all groups. • γ01 and γk1 are the effects of the group-level predictor Zj on the intercept and slope for the kth feature. • u0j and ukj are the random effects for the intercept and slope for the kth feature in group j.

Level 1 (Within-Group) Model: At this level, we’re modeling the relationship between the specific metrics (outcome variable) and the features of the LLMs (predictor variables) within each group. Each group in our context is formed by the rule that any finetuned version of another LLM is part of the same higher level group. Clear separation is evident between LLMs that incorporate RLHF and those that do not. LLMs with RLHF demonstrate behaviors that appear, on average, roughly 2× more similar to human behavior compared to the models without. However, it is important to note that while UMAP space retains some global structure, it is primarily used for visualization purposes. Consequently, we also analyzed the average distances before dimensionality reduction (using normalized feature vectors), observing a 11.7% average decrease in L2-Norm distance for models with RLHF (Figure 3B). Conclusion: Hypothesis is supported.

Our investigation initially focused on probabilistic reasoning, which is a fundamental cognitive ability in decisionmaking. This ability facilitates the optimal integration of new information with pre-existing knowledge. We used the performance metric from the probabilistic reasoning experiment, namely posterior accuracy, which is calculated as one minus the deviation from the Bayes optimal prediction for each task. As depicted in Figure 6A, both CoT and SB techniques generally enhanced probabilistic reasoning compared to their base models, with CoT showing an average increase of 9.01% and SB showing an increase of 3.10%.

Furthermore, we discovered that model-basedness, a critical aspect of reasoning and planning, is significantly augmented by both CoT and SB techniques, as shown in Figure 6B. Specifically, CoT demonstrated a 64.59% increase, while SB showed a substantial increase of 118.59%. Interestingly, a closer examination of the figures and the numerical data suggests that CoT is more effective for probabilistic reasoning, while SB excels in enhancing modelbasedness. This observation aligns with the notion that step-by-step thinking can aid mathematical reasoning (Kojima et al., 2022) while abstracting a problem by taking a step back can foster a better representation of the problem’s abstract structure. We found that the number of parameters indeed had a significant influence on performance (β = 0.277 ± 0.39, z = 14.1, p < 0.001; see Figure 4A). However, the size of the training dataset and the use of code training data did not have a substantial impact. One possible explanation for this could be that the quality of the training data, rather than its sheer volume, plays a more determining role in performance, as well as that larger models also tend to be trained on larger datasets.
